title: GitHub Enterprise Governance Automation
subtitle: Building automation for GitHub Enterprise Cloud at scale — org-level secrets management, third-party Action allowlisting, repository governance via identity platform, and a Python CLI toolkit for member/hooks/SSO/identity operations.
overview: At a Fortune 500 company, the CI Platform team owned GitHub Enterprise Cloud organization administration for 2,000+ engineers. This meant managing org-level secrets, allowlisting third-party Actions, controlling repository access through the identity governance platform, and building automation to make all of this self-service.

I worked on building and maintaining the automation layer: a declarative secrets catalog with validation, an action allowlist with dual-team approval, and a Python CLI toolkit (Click-based) for member management, webhook operations, SSO/identity sync, and GitHub App lifecycle management.

The result: engineers could request and get org-level resources through PR-based workflows instead of manual tickets, supply chain security was enforced through automated validation, and GitHub governance became auditable and reversible through Git history.
challenge: The Problem: GitHub Enterprise Cloud governance at scale requires managing hundreds of repositories, thousands of team memberships, org-level secrets, third-party Action policies, and service accounts — all while maintaining security compliance and audit trails.

Before automation, these were manual processes: engineers filed tickets to request org secrets, security reviews happened in Slack threads, and repository access was managed through ad-hoc group memberships. There was no single source of truth, no automated validation, and no easy way to audit who had access to what.

The supply chain risk was particularly acute: without an allowlist, any engineer could reference any third-party Action in their workflows — including potentially malicious ones. Security needed visibility and control without blocking developer velocity.
solution: The secrets catalog is a configuration-as-code system where each org-level secret is a JSON file with name, assigned_repos, visibility (selected/all/private), and metadata. The validation workflow enforces strict rules: alphanumeric + underscore only, no reserved prefixes, no leading digit, assigned_repos required, visibility-consistent repo lists. Auto-sorting of assigned_repos keeps diffs clean for PR reviews.

The action allowlist is the supply chain security control plane. A policy file defines which third-party Actions and reusable workflows are permitted in the org. On merge to main, the policy syncs to GitHub org settings via API. Dual-team approval (CI Platform + Security) ensures proper review. Validation includes license compliance checks and overlap detection for redundant patterns.

The admin CLI toolkit is a Python CLI (Click-based) for GitHub organization operations: member management, repository webhook operations, SAML SSO/identity sync integration, and GitHub App lifecycle management. It wraps the GitHub REST and GraphQL APIs into repeatable commands using PyGithub instead of one-off UI changes.

All three systems follow the same pattern: Git as the source of truth, PR as the review mechanism, CI as the enforcement layer, and merge-to-main as the deployment event. This makes every policy change auditable, reversible, and traceable.

architecture.heading: Secrets Catalog
content: Each secret is a JSON file under a Secrets/ directory with name, assigned_repos (sorted list), visibility, and flags. The validation workflow runs on every PR: JSON syntax check, duplicate name detection, business rule validation, and auto-commit of sorted assigned_repos.

Business rules encode GitHub's naming constraints plus org-specific policies: reserved prefixes, visibility 'selected' cannot use wildcard patterns, non-selected visibilities must not list specific repos. A cleanup script handles housekeeping when repos leave the org.

architecture.heading: Supply Chain Security
content: The allowlist contains flags (github_owned_allowed, verified_allowed) and patterns_allowed (owner/repo@ref patterns). Validation includes: format linting via jq (sort|unique), overlap detection (finding redundant or conflicting globs), and license compliance (checking for problematic licenses).

On merge to main, the sync workflow pushes the policy to GitHub org settings via CLI. A backup workflow preserves policy snapshots. The entire flow — PR review → CI validation → merge → API push — is auditable through Git history.

architecture.heading: Repository Governance via Identity Platform
content: The identity governance platform manages repository ownership and access through YAML files. Each repo has a type, owner (team), additional_admins (teams), outside_collaborators (with username, reason, role, expiration), and optionally archived status.

A base permission decision established 'write' as the default for all org members (aligning with innersource culture), reducing repository roles to read/write/admin. This eliminated unnecessary composite groups and custom roles that existed only to provision basic access.

timeline.title: Secrets Catalog
timeline.description: Built the declarative secrets catalog with JSON-per-secret model, validation workflow, auto-sorting, and business rule enforcement. Set up PR-based governance for org secrets.

timeline.title: Allowlist System
timeline.description: Built the action allowlist with dual-team approval, license compliance checks, overlap detection, and automated policy sync to GitHub org settings.

timeline.title: Toolkit CLI
timeline.description: Built the Python CLI (Click) for member management, webhook operations, SSO/identity sync. Integrated with GitHub App authentication and GraphQL API via PyGithub.

timeline.title: Access Model Simplification
timeline.description: Implemented base permission ADR: default write for all members, reduced roles to read/write/admin, deprecated unnecessary composite groups and custom roles.

timeline.title: Integration & Documentation
timeline.description: Cross-linked all repos to internal documentation. Published guides for onboarding, service account requests, and notification management.

learnings: Configuration-as-code makes governance reviewable. When org secrets and Action allowlists are JSON files in Git, every change gets PR-reviewed, CI-validated, and merge-deployed. A bad policy change is a git revert, not a manual console cleanup with uncertain blast radius.

Dual-team approval is the right pattern for supply chain security. CI Platform understands the operational impact; Security understands the risk implications. Neither alone has the full picture. The allowlist's dual-approval requirement prevents both security blind spots and operational surprises.

Automated sorting prevents merge conflicts in collaborative files. Both secrets and allowlist auto-commit sorted JSON on PRs. This eliminates an entire category of merge conflicts and keeps diffs reviewable — reviewers see actual policy changes, not reordering noise.

Self-service through PRs scales better than tickets. Every governance operation — requesting a secret, adding an Action, changing repo access — goes through a PR. Engineers get what they need in hours (PR review time), not days (ticket SLA), and every change is traceable.
